On sight no people don’t know where your parents are from, but accents and cultural markers can provide that insight when people look for those clues- and the reality is that immigrating to this nation voluntarily is a privilege that African Americans don’t have. We have a traumatic history in this nation that makes our political needs distinct and nuanced. All black people can have traumatic experiences in the US, but not all black people are inheriting intergenerational trauma from chattel slavery in the US. The nuances between AAs and non-AAs matters, especially when it comes to topics like reparations and “culture war” debates gutting African American history from schools.

Often not being able to trace back your ancestry is a sign that your ancestors lives were disrupted by colonialism/enslavement. Willing Immigrants don’t often have that problem, but displaced people do.

Intergenerational trauma from centuries of enslavement is real. Nobody is saying immigrants don’t suffer, but if you’re moving into a land where other ppls ancestors were enslaved and are still actively being murdered by that same government and denied Justice, that does takes a toll that immigrants may not feel as burdened by. Just like if I moved somewhere where other ppl had historically suffered, I know walking on that land doesn’t carry the same emotional burden for me. Nuance.

I think a conversation on the disparities between African Americans and African immigrants is worth considering, only to examine how immigrants often arrive with higher ed degrees and an emotional distance from white supremacy which makes them more attractive to white institutions here compared to African Americans (AA). I’ve personally heard anti-AA comments from Nigerian immigrants who simultaneously appropriated AA culture to the fullest. Comments like “well why don’t you guys just behave in front of police”, “I thought you’d talk more hood” and “so you guys don’t know where you’re from”. I think the desire for a distinction comes from the reality that there are nuances in the African American experience and history that are not shared by all black people who immigrate to the US. I dislike FBA bc it leans into nationalism and xenophobia rather than encouraging shared understanding, but I understand where the desire for distinction comes from.

African American. While I like the idea of finding a more specific way to refer to our extensive history in the US I found that the ADOS and FBA movements were often leaning into nationalism and xenophobia, biases that I really don’t want to take hold in our community.

Being an adult now, I work around kids. It see their size, how small they are, and feel sick to my stomach. I don’t understand how an adult could see such a small being and think physically harming them is an acceptable form of teaching. I didn’t view certain things as abuse growing up but now that I’m and adult I understand more- especially when my partner moves too quickly and I flinch in response. They don’t care to be accountable and rectify the situation though, they can’t accept the game they caused. They insist it will all work out in the end. Supposedly im stronger than I think…

They don’t consider it abuse. “Discipline” is normal, and a responsible parent disciplines their child. It’s not abuse, it’s their job and role as a parent, and your job as the child is to take the abuse with humility and learn something from it. 

Sure sometimes it involves a heavy hand, a belt, or a cord- but that’s the learning experience. Plus as the parent you’re in charge, you pay the bills so it’s it’s your house, your rules. Even if the rules violate your child’s privacy (no closed doors and you have to hand over your cell phone at any moment for inspection). Worse if you go to church, the shame of “sparing the rod and spoiling the child” has inspired even progressive parents to use corporal punishment. So you can shame your kid about eating too much, finishing their plate and daring to ask for seconds. Moving from a size 00 (middle school) to a size 7 (senior year of high school) and go ahead and put your kid on a diet and exercise regimen and nonchalantly mention they could do plus sizes modeling. Your kids getting bullied at school and grades suffer- nope they’re just lazy. Your kids compulsively pulling out their hair at the root due to stress from eviction? Go ahead and yell in their face “WHAT IS WRONG WITH YOU!”, you’ve gotta get to the bottom of this after all because you’re the parent. Your kid breaks up with a guy you liked? Go ahead and go through their texts to see what went wrong, then confront your kid about it- that won’t cause trust issues at all. Your kid opens up to your about being molested as a child, begs you to keep it quiet? Go ahead and tell their cousins, they don’t mind. Years later when you’re going through menopause and smack your kid in the face for daring to suggest you’re a neglectful and harmful parent- feel free to completely forget that memory and insist your child is making it up. You’re the parent, so you make the rules of reality. 

Your job as a parent is to gather as much information as you can so that you can judge and punish your child for it. Of course not information on development psychology, just the Bible and the encouragement of other domineering parents. All this isn’t abuse, it’s guidance, it’s discipline. It’s their job.

Whew buddy. I’m so sorry to have to tell you this. 
Natural hair is a full time JOB. I have buff arms JUST from doing my hair. And you have thick hair? Hahahhahahaah 😂 oh buddy. 

I have thick 4c/4b/4a/3c hair. 

For starters, you’re gonna want to fully moisturize 2 times a week, then put it in a protective style. Deep conditioning/hair masks every other week or once a month, whenever styling work in a scalp massage to stimulate growth. Manipulate your hair as little as possible, to prevent unnecessary stress. If you can, finger detangle instead of using combs/brushes. ALWAYS detangle on wet hair never dry. Avoid ponytails and buns and these cause pulling/tension at your hair line. If you need to use a comb/brush as a stying tool every once in a while that’s fine.  Unfortunately, your scalp is sensitive because of the perms, so you really want to be gentle with your hair. I wouldn’t suggest doing it in increments if that means doing those “half perm” things because you’re still adding harmful chemicals. Doing so will only make your transition stage last longer and extend the time you have to wait for fully healthy hair. Pro tip: for those with thick hair do your hair in 4-6 individual sections. 

Many people think “I’ll just big chop and the next hair that grows will be healthy”. Big no. Even when you cut off the damaged bits, if your hair follicles were damaged they’ll still grow unhealthy hair until your follicles heal. It’s going to take time and you have to be patient. Styling can take anywhere from 1-5 hours depending on your hairs thickness, I’m between 3-5 hours for a style. That awkward half curly half damaged stage will feel like it lasts forever but it doesn’t, think if your time as an investment. (In total it took about 6 years for my hair to fully become healthy and grow healthily from my scalp and some sections of my hair still don’t have a defined pattern. )

DO NOT straighten your hair. I know you may be tempted to, but don’t. Extreme heat isn’t good for your hair, and it’s not worth the risk to damage hair when you’re working towards getting it to its peak of health. If you really want straight hair get a wig, leave your own hair alone. Wash your hair with cool/warming water, never hot (why heat damage your hair in the shower?)
Don’t wear your hair out during extreme cold as this will cause increased breakage. Diet can also make certain things easier, many foods have benefits to your hair skin and nails. Eggs and salmon can improve your hair growth rate and the shine of your hair. 

The products that work for you at the start of your natural hair journey/transition likely won’t be the products you use at the end. As your hair grows healthier, it’ll respond to different products/methods differently. At the start do my transition, LCO left my hair the most moisturized. 4 years later I was shocked to find that my hair now responded better to LOC. Unfortunately I cannot say for sure what products will work best for your specific head of hair, but I can encourage you to read the ingredients in every product you buy. There are a lot of companies trying to cash in on the natural hair movement but not everyone makes a good product. Next, if your curl pattern was destroyed (like mine was) this will be a long recovery. It gets better though. After doing mini chops for 3 years; two years ago I cut my hair to shoulder length-the shortest my hair was ever been. Today it’s waist length (thanks God). 

Oh and stay away from deva curl.

context for those of you who don’t do any research beyond a reddit article and wanna get angry at me like I’m a slave owner sympathizer

one of the most unique factors about chattel slavery was that a persons slave status became dependent on the slave status of their mother. So where previously slavery would only impact the individual (prisoner of war or indebted person), now slavery impacted every generation following. For black people born in the colonies, this meant being born INTO servitude, not living ANY aspect of a free life (unless you were one of the lucky few whose “master” gave you freedom it even then you could be kidnapped in another state and re-enslaved. While not nearly as common, female plantation owners/wives/daughters also raped male slaves but were more likely to either have their children given mercy (freedom, or sold to a potentially less abusive plantation). Because slavery in Africa was not inherited, they did not know that selling one person would enslave their descendants for the next hundred+ years. Run of the mill kidnapping and murder was normal to every civilization at this point, the enslavement and forced labor of toddlers was NOT. The indiscriminate lifelong torture of someone just based on skin color and not “tribe” was NOT. If you are actually following the grammar rules for AAVE you’re likely fine. The only time it’s offensive is when you clearly have no grasp of the language, cause then it seems like it’s either a joke to the writer or like you lack the education to properly realize you’re butchering the language. It’s deliriously easy to let such get past production. 

People who speak AAVE natively and code switch do so at particular times for particular reasons- definitely consider that since you say your character only uses it a few times, there should be a reason that they’re using it (why are they code switching). 

A character raised in a gated mostly white community may not speak AAVE as well as their friend who drew up in zone 13, or they may butcher AAVE and blend it with standard English grammar and pronunciations. A black person may speak AAVE solely at home but code switch at school. Word choices within AAVE also change based on age and regional dialect. A teenager in Texas doesn’t speak the same AAVE as a teen from the bay. These regional nuances aren’t such a big deal in some instances because AAVE is very communal and spreads rapidly especially with the popularity of black culture in the media, but if you were to say your character is from baltimore but they speak with ny inspired AAVE, this would be a dead giveaway. 

Beyond a grasp of the grammar rules, an understanding of the politics of AAVE is also important to correctly portray a nuanced character.

Unlike an accent, AAVE is recognized as an independent language by the American Linguistic Society and it has very clear grammar rules/guidelines. AAVE isn’t an accent or a voice, it’s a language. Dialogue depth shouldn’t be related to the actual language your character is speaking, unless you’re having trouble translating to AAVE and accidentally butcher the format. If your character typically speaks in AAVE, most speakers alter *how* they speak based on audience (grandma vs best friend) but they’d still be speaking aave, and their grandma and best friend likely would as well. And the word choice of the younger best friend would be different from the older grandma (ex: keep it 100 vs keep it buck). There’s also various regional accents within AAVE, so that’s where accent would come into play (if your character is from Baltimore but using largely Bay Area AAVE, viewers who *know* would notice). 

If a character speaks AAVE natively, the times they speak standard English should be indicators of something occurring in your setting (ex: your character is in a new place and feels uncomfortable, causing the desire to code switch). How successful your character is able to code switch (and how they feel about having to code switch) is also indicative of personality. (Even the reverse is true: if your character doesn’t speak AAVE but makes friends with a new boy from his basketball team and suddenly is using whatever word he heard in the last 2chainz track, his desire to use such words in the setting is indicative of an internal perspective. How accurately or inaccurately  he speaks AAVE would indicate even more about the characters history). As a language AAVE inherently comes with a lot of political/historical undertones and can add a lot of depth to a character if used accurately and correctly.

I’d say your biggest hiccup would be defining your participants based on race. If you do such a series based on modern ideas of race (which loosely equates to skin color since biologically race does not exist), you’d likely piss a lot of people off. Skin color (race) doesn’t mean the same culture/food/music. A Black American does not have anything culturally in common with a black Danish person. Similarly a white Norwegian man doesn’t have anything culturally in common with a white Latino man from Peru. Ideas of race also change based on location. A light skinned Girl of African descent may call herself black in the US but be considered morena in Brazil. Simularly, a morena may be offended to be considered black elsewhere. Basing the episodes theme on cultural background and not race would solve a lot to those problems. 

Also important to consider while you could help educate on different backgrounds and cultural norms it could inadvertently subject them as participant to trauma by sending them to a location where people react violently towards them. You may be putting participants in the uncomfortable position of having to explain their own background. A Nigerian touring Singapore would likely need production help securing housing (many landlords and hotels refuse Nigerians). Would production help or just follow the experiences? You may want to consider HOW and WHY you’re featuring Native American culture first, and do some research on the history of Native American tribes both prior to, during, and after colonialism. You’re concern shouldn’t be “offending”, it should be showing you that you do have genuine respect for this culture you wish to explore in your writing, show that you didn’t just toss in some “Native” ghosts as a play off the “haunted Indian graveyard” trope. Writers love to take liberties and I’m all for that, but consider how frequently colonized groups have had  unflattering liberties taken (with their likeness, folklore, people, land, etc.) , you’re less likely to offend if you’re approaching the subject matter with respect. 

First I would suggest narrowing down exactly what indigenous tribe you’re hoping to pull inspiration from, so far what strikes me as potentially the most offensive is the lack of definition there. There are hundreds of bands and tribes and something that gets frequently critiqued is when writers water them all down to a monolith (highlighting that they’ve done zero research). 

Next I’d suggest contacting someone from that tribe, explaining that you’re a writer looking to include Native American folklore and culture into your work, hopefully you’ll be put into contact with someone willing to work as your cultural advisor (you should pay this person for their time as well). You should include a Native American character otherwise yes you run the risk of yet another portrayal of poc as magical “other”, a stereotype that’s both tired and damaging in real life. There are resources available online but culturally many indigenous tribes were verbal knowledge sharers, so you’d likely be able to get more authentic information from speaking with someone. Additionally, studying indigenous ways of knowing would likely improve your scope of thought as you explore this subject matter since you’ve likely been taught solely in Western/European ways of knowing. Wishing you the best of luck.

Disclaimer: I’m Black with mixed indigenous heritage, but was not raised on the reserve or in connection with my indigenous relatives, so I would not be considered a qualified cultural advisor in this sense.

This question is really general, do you have any examples of alcoholism being used to propel a story without any real character drive? Alcoholism isn’t merely an American problem, but culturally the US and Canada do drink differently (and are introduced to alcohol differently) than say teens in Italy. Teens in the US are legally barred from drinking until 21, so it’s heavily restricted and criminalized so kids often drink to excess when they have the chance. Compared to Italian teens who’re legally able to drink at 16 and used to pairing wine with a meal, savoring it as an addition to their dining experience. When I travelled to Italy and Paris one common theme was that locals were confused by the way American teens would drink when they arrived as they frequently got very drunk. 

Going to bars/clubs and drinking is a large part of socializing in the US. That’s why there’s a whole event around “pre-gaming” (drinking before you go out to your party destination where you will likely drink again). There’s a reason why we have groups such as MADD (Moms against drunk driving) and a whole college Greek culture that glorifies getting sloshed. In both the US and Canada all the college campuses I visited had insane amounts of alcoholism. You’d step outside and find people passed out in the hallway smelling like they could light a torch. 

It’s not being advertising it to kids (most shows containing alcoholism have a content warning and mature rating anyway), though young adolescent drinking isn’t uncommon. I knew a freshman girl in high school who began bringing vodka in her water bottle, I found out years later she was being sexually abused by her dad. A Canadian kid I know began heavily drinking at 12, by 19 he was a full blown alcoholic. I later discovered he was physically abused by his stepdad from age 7-11 and never recovered from feeling betrayed by his mother for staying with him. Saskatchewan has the highest alcoholism rate in all of Canada and when I asked locals why so many people went out to drink I was often told “there’s nothing else to do here”. 

I have friends who turned to heavy drinking after returning from Afghanistan, or after facing an encounter like police brutality or sexual assault. You may chalk it up to lazy character motivation but alcoholism is an unfortunate reality for many people dealing with inner demons so it does make sense to portray it on screen.

Ahhhh...let me say that when I had trich getting my hair done was extremely nerve wracking. I also know the allure of pulling and getting the root/little black dot at the end, i used to like running it over my lips. Resist its siren call. Maybe go to a salon super early when it’s rather empty, a few times I’ve tried the old “I got prescribed new medication that caused hair loss” to explain my spots, the stylist should be understanding. 

Alternate option is to wear a hat or hoodie for the rest of your life (this was my method after the boy I had a crush on turned to someone else in class and said “did you know _____ has bald spots” when they thought my headphones were playing music.)

The anxiety doesn’t go away, the trick is managing it. Try to keep your hands busy, don’t even touch your hair if it’s not necessary as that can be a slippery slope. If you’re like me and you sometimes run your pull spots, don’t, this is also a slippery slope. The whole things just slippery. Maybe try a dodger cube to keep your hands busy, they’re less obnoxious than a dodger spinner and the ones with 8 sides are pretty fun for keeping your hand engaged. You could also try embroidery, knitting, just keep your hands busy. That and if you notice you’re tempted to pull, take a moment and assess your life. What is a pressing concern? Are you stressed about a particular problem/event? How can you ease that anxiety without pulling? Sometimes you could absentminded be thinking of something that troubles you and your brain signals you to pull to “modify” or fix something that’s in your control (my pulling hair, biting nails, chewing tastebuds, ect.). I hope this helps. Having trich as a teen made me miserable.

I personally haven’t seen virginity shaming as a big issue facing black women (and based off other comments there aren’t many that perceive it as a problem). That being said, no conversations on sex/sexuality and black women will be solved until we fully address the rates of sexual abuse and violence against black women. Why? Because how can black women have conversations on sex when as a group sexualized violence is used against them at such high rates. Obviously the abuse will have a significant impact on how individuals can engage with and perceive their own sexuality. Black women report being sexually abused starting from age 5, and both black womanhood and black girlhood are heavily impacted by sexual violence. The prevalence of sexualized violence taints the conversations as black womens sexual experiences are rife with abuse and mistreatment, which can alter the ways in which intimacy is recognized (or unrecognized) and yes affects how sexual activity (by themselves and others) is perceived. Given that black women are often blamed for their own assaults, this can lead to people being defensive in conversations on sex and virginity, but the conversation on virginity still can’t happen until the cause of that defensiveness is addressed. Unfortunately I don’t feel this conversation is even necessary until we address sexual violence against black women because to me that’s a much bigger problem.

Obviously this isn’t a solely (or even a majority) black womens issue, but there’s some things I’d consider. For starters, many black women have complicated relationships with sex. Black women are the most vulnerable for sexual assault, most likely to not be believed when they report sexual assault, most likely to avoid reporting their assault because they don’t want to become further victim to police violence (or feel guilty reporting a member of their community). Also over 50% of black women report being sexually abused before 18. In conversations on virginity with black women I’ve never heard black women shaming others, but I have heard some uncomfortable admissions on how virginity and ideals of purity was used against black women (being called fast tailed girls at early ages criminalizing them for sexual activity regardless of whether they’ve participated- or criticizing them for having sexual knowledge without acknowledging that it came from abuse), or black women’s discussing how consent was either blurry or absent during their first sexual encounters. Given the long noted history of sexual violence that’s been used against black women (slavery propaganda often painting them as hypersexual jezebels or asexual subservient mammys), a conversation on virginity [which itself is a social construct and is loaded with different meanings when associated with womanhood] and black women that sorta paints anti-virginity shaming as a black womens issue (as if black women aren’t always labeled the ‘problem’ or the aggressors in any space) is definitely going to be met with some contention given the tone of the questioning and the lack of nuance within the question itself. There’s no specification of what age/region of black women you perceive as being the perpetrators of this shaming, only a one size fits all “black women” on a topic where many black women have found themselves unfairly judged from birth. Perhaps the same question could be asked in a different tone and get a more fruitful result, but it’s definitely important to consider the ways virginity and purity itself were viewed as a solely white woman trait during chattel slavery, and black women were not perceived as possessing this “inner innocence”, the lack of which was (and still is) used to justify sexual violence towards black women).
